symbols.id: Creating an instance from the console
pseudo: #> The person submits the form -> instance_actions.submit_create_instance

They choose a name, a number of CPUs, an amount of memory and the size of the boot disk. The console checks the name and sizes, and that the project has enough of its quota left, before sending anything.
#> The API checks who is asking -> POST /v1/instances
The person must be signed in and be a collaborator or an admin of the project. A viewer is refused.
#> The API checks the request -> instances.create_instance
It checks the name and sizes again, that no instance or boot disk in the project has the name, and that the project's quota has room. Stopped and failed instances still count against the quota.
#> The instance gets an address and a boot disk -> rack_store.address_allocate
One address is taken from the rack's pool and a boot disk is created, attached to the instance. If no address is free the request is refused and nothing is created.
#> The instance is recorded as creating
The API answers at once. The console shows the instance as "creating".
It asks for the instance once a second, for up to 30 seconds, and stops when it is running or failed.
#> The rack finds room, or does not -> placement.place_instance

Three seconds after it was created, the instance is given a place if the rack has the CPUs and memory free, and becomes running. If the rack is full it becomes failed, with a reason the console shows.

The console reloads the project so the usage is right, then says the instance is running at its address, or that it failed and what to try. A failed instance keeps its disk, address and quota, and can be started again or deleted.
symbols.doc: What happens between submitting the create-instance form and seeing the instance running.

pseudo: #> The person presses Stop and confirms -> instance_actions.stop_instance
The console offers this only for a running instance, and asks first because whatever runs on the instance is interrupted.
#> The API checks who is asking and the state -> POST /v1/instances/{instance}/stop

A collaborator or an admin of the project may stop it. Only a running instance can be stopped. Stopping one that is already stopping or stopped changes nothing, and one that is being created, is starting or has failed is refused.
#> The instance is marked as stopping -> instances.stop_instance
It still holds its place on the rack while it stops.
It asks for the instance once a second until it is stopped.
Three seconds later it is stopped, and its CPUs and memory on the rack are free for others. It keeps its disks, its address and its share of the project's quota.
symbols.doc: What happens when a person stops a running instance.

/// Every way a request can be refused. The console reads `error_code` to choose what to tell the person.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum ApiError {
    Unauthenticated,
    SessionExpired,
    InvalidCredentials,
    AccountLocked { until: u64 },
    Forbidden { needed: ProjectRole },
    ProjectNotFound,
    InstanceNotFound,
    DiskNotFound,
    UserNotFound,
    InvalidRequest(String),
    ProjectNameTaken,
    InstanceNameTaken,
    DiskNameTaken,
    ProjectNotEmpty { instances: usize, disks: usize },
    LastAdmin,
    QuotaExceeded { resource: String, requested: u32, available: u32 },
    AddressPoolExhausted,
    InstanceBusy { state: InstanceState },
    InstanceNotRunning { state: InstanceState },
    InstanceNotStopped { state: InstanceState },
    DiskAttached,
    TooManyDisks { limit: usize },
}

domains.doc: One rack of machines. Running instances use its CPUs and memory, and every instance holds one address from its pool. A project's quota says what it may reserve; the rack decides whether there is room right now. An instance that finds no room fails, and can be started again later.

The web console. Each thing a person does, such as submitting a form or pressing Stop, is one action. An action checks what it can in the browser, asks the API, then shows the outcome in plain words. Changes that take time are followed by asking the API again every second.

domains.tag: Who you are and what you may do
domains.doc: People sign in with a name and password and get a session that lasts eight hours. Five wrong passwords in a row lock the account for 15 minutes. On each project a person is a viewer, a collaborator or an admin, or has no role and cannot see the project at all.

domains.tag: Groups of resources with a quota
domains.doc: A project holds instances and disks, and sets a quota of CPUs, memory and storage they share. Whoever creates a project is its admin. A project can be deleted only once it is empty. Projects, instances and disks follow one rule for names.

An instance is a virtual machine with CPUs, memory, a boot disk and an address. It is created as "creating" and is running or failed a few seconds later. Starting and stopping also take a few seconds. Only a running instance can be stopped, and only a stopped or failed one can be started or deleted.

A disk is storage in a project, attached to one instance or to none. Every instance has a boot disk that is created and deleted with it. Other disks are created on their own, attached while the instance is stopped, and kept when the instance is deleted.
